transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-18
Start: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jordan (Redwood SE), Samir (Tidal Head of Platform), Elena (SRE Lead), Noah (Security), Claire (PM)

Auto-generated summary:
Tidal Commerce is evaluating Redwood for inference across checkout personalization and fraud detection features. Primary concerns are deterministic failover behavior, multi-region routing for read/path redundancy, and ensuring Private/VPC options meet compliance. They are leaning toward a pilot that tests hotpath fallbacks and regional steering under simulated outages.

Topics:
- Fallback policies and model variant mapping
- Multi-region routing and session affinity
- SLAs and degradation modes (graceful degradation vs errors)
- Private/VPC onboarding, KMS, audit logs
- Benchmark plan for failover and perf tests

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick round of intros?
[00:08] Samir (Tidal): Samir, Head of Platform at Tidal Commerce. We own the infra for personalization and checkout.
[00:12] Elena (Tidal SRE): Elena, SRE lead. I care about uptime and clear failover behaviors.
[00:16] Noah (Tidal Sec): Noah, security. I'll mainly audit data paths, KMS, and retention.
[00:21] Claire (PM): Claire, product — running the personalization roadmap.
[00:23] Maya (Redwood): Great. Jordan, quick intro?
[00:25] Jordan (Redwood SE): Jordan, I run infra integration for Dedicated and Private customers, do benchmarks and runbooks.
[00:30] Maya (Redwood): Goals for today — understand your reliability needs, mapping of critical paths, and whether Hosted/Dedicated/Private fit. Also identify concrete pilot steps.
[00:38] Samir: High level — we have two hotpaths. One is checkout personalization (low latency, p90 < 60ms ideally). The other is fraud model scoring that can tolerate slightly higher latency but must never silently drop requests.
[00:50] Elena: We need predictable failover. If a region goes noisy or a node flaps, we want clear, documented behavior — either synchronous fallback to another region or safe degradation with cached output, not weird 500 spikes.
[01:05] Jordan: Understood. Redwood supports policy-based routing, you can choose latency-first or cost-first, and we do automatic fallback to compatible model variants. For example, if your primary is a 7B fp16 in us-east-1 and that capacity is full, we can route to a quantized 7B variant in us-west-2 or fall back to cached prefix results.
[01:28] Noah: Quantized variants — what's the difference to accuracy, and are those considered 'fallback' so we get audit logs when that happens? We need to know when the model variant changes for compliance.
[01:39] Jordan: Yes. We label variant changes in audit logs. Accuracy delta depends on quantization profile — for most of our public baselines it's within a 1-2% quality window on ranking tasks, but for sensitive fraud models we'd recommend doing a short eval set as part of the pilot.
[01:56] Claire: If a fallback causes even a 2% model drift in checkout recommendations, that could impact conversions — we need guardrails.
[02:05] Maya: Totally. That’s why pilots usually include both perf and quality checks. We'll propose a canary + automatic rollback policy: if certain evaluation metrics drop by X, route back or quarantine.
[02:18] Samir: How deterministic is the routing? We want session affinity so that for the lifetime of a checkout session requests stay in the same region unless there's a failure.
[02:28] Jordan: We support session affinity via sticky keys at the gateway. You can opt for session-key hashing mapped to region pools. Failover only triggers if health checks fail or capacity is exhausted per policy.
[02:40] Elena: What's the health check cadence? We don't want micro-failovers during minor GC pauses.
[02:45] Jordan: Health checks are configurable. Default 5s probe with 3 consecutive failures by default; you can increase windows to avoid flaps. We also expose event streams and tracing to attach to your existing observability.
[02:58] Noah: Regarding hosting modes — what are tradeoffs between Hosted and Dedicated for our use case? Security-wise we prefer VPC isolation, but cost and latency matter.
[03:08] Maya: Hosted gives fastest time-to-value; Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools and private networking from our end. Private (VPC or on-prem) gives you the most control over networking and keys. For compliance you'd likely want Dedicated with VPC peering or Private deployment depending on audit requirements.
[03:26] Noah: KMS integration — can we use our HSM-backed keys?
[03:30] Jordan: Yes, Private supports customer-managed keys (Cloud KMS or HSM) and we can integrate via KMS envelopes. We'll note that in the security pack.
[03:37] Claire: Do we lose streaming responses if we route to a quantized fallback or different region? We rely on streaming to render progressive UI.
[03:44] Jordan: Streaming is supported across variants and regions; however, there can be additional latency due to cross-region network. We can measure that in the bench.
[03:53] Samir: Let's talk SLAs. We need to map critical endpoints to an SLA and understand degradation modes. We don't expect 100% perfect, but clear p99, p95, and an SLO for successful responses during partial outages.
[04:07] Maya: Our standard Hosted SLA is 99.9% availability; Dedicated can be contracted at higher tiers. For partial degradation, we offer circuit-breaker policies: fail closed (return an error), fail open (return cached/approximate), or degrade to cheaper variant. These are policy-configurable per route.
[04:26] Elena: For fraud scoring, we can't return cached stale scores. So fail closed for that route, but with alerting to fallback pipeline (async replay). For personalization, failing open with a conservative default is acceptable.
[04:40] Jordan: Good pattern. We'll show how to set per-route policies and alert hooks. Also, for fail-closed we recommend a secondary async path that logs the request and replays it once capacity recovers.
[04:53] Noah: How granular are audit logs — do they show which fallback happened, timestamp, decision reason?
[04:58] Jordan: Logs include the routing decision, model variant, region, latency, trace id, and reason code (health, capacity, policy). They can be exported to your SIEM.
[05:10] Samir: One concern — cold-starts for on-demand Hosted instances. We've seen long tail latency with some providers during scale up.
[05:19] Jordan: We mitigate with warm pools and predictive scaling based on traffic patterns and token distribution. Dedicated avoids cold starts because capacity is reserved. We'll include warmup tuning in the bench plan.
[05:33] Claire: What's the pilot shape you usually recommend for these reliability checks?
[05:37] Maya: Typical pilot: 2-3 week test, include synthetic traffic that simulates failures (region blackhole, increased latency), plus real traffic shadowing. Bench includes failover time, correctness checks, and cost delta analysis.
[05:50] Elena: We want to run a blackout where we cut us-east-1 for 15 minutes and ensure traffic routes to us-west-2 without losing more than N% successful responses.
[05:58] Jordan: We'll script that. Also recommend step-down tests: degrade CPU on host, kill a node, simulate GK pause, etc.\n[06:09] Samir: Are there rate limits or throttles that could cause silent drops? We need backpressure behavior defined.
[06:16] Jordan: We expose quota windows and token-based rate limits. If you hit thresholds we return 429 with a retry-after. For critical routes you can configure burst buckets and reserve capacity in Dedicated.
[06:28] Noah: Encryption at rest and in transit — we need confirmation data never leaves region unencrypted.
[06:33] Jordan: Data in transit is TLS. At rest, we support customer-managed keys and regional storage; cross-region replication is optional and can be disabled for compliance.
[06:45] Claire: How are model rollouts handled — we want gradual canaries and automatic rollback with quality gating.
[06:51] Maya: Console supports canary traffic percentages, metric gates tied to quality tests, and automatic rollback on regression. You can bind your own eval sets.
[07:01] Elena: On the ops side, what observability hooks do we get? Traces, per-token cost, latency breakdown by model stage?
[07:08] Jordan: Yes — per-token latency, kernel time, queuing time, and model variant. We also provide traces compatible with open telemetry and per-route dashboards.
[07:18] Samir: We need to confirm token accounting during failovers — we don't want duplicate billing if a request is retried in another region.
[07:26] Jordan: Good point. Our system attributes billing to the final successful completion and emits retry reason tags. For some internal retries we can suppress billing if desired; we'll include options in the pilot contract.
[07:39] Claire: For Dedicated, can we pin GPUs to single-tenant nodes for low jitter?
[07:44] Jordan: Yes, Dedicated offers isolated GPU pools; you can choose single-tenant instances. That reduces jitter but increases cost.
[07:52] Noah: One more security question — SSO and RBAC. We'll need SAML + SCIM provisioning and role separation for ops vs devs.
[07:59] Maya: Supported. We'll send the SAML/SCIM integration guide.
[08:03] Samir: Let's talk long tail degradation: during a gradual regional network degradation, can we do progressive traffic shift rather than abrupt failover?
[08:12] Jordan: We support weighted traffic shifting over a configured window, with automated rollback if error rate spikes. That avoids large blips during partial network issues.
[08:22] Elena: Will weighted shift respect session affinity?
[08:25] Jordan: Yes, session affinity is preserved until a failover policy triggers; weighted shifting is applied to new sessions or as configured.
[08:35] Samir: What's the observability latency for health events — how fast will we see that a node is unhealthy in the console?
[08:41] Jordan: Health events stream within seconds; our console shows real-time events and we provide webhooks for immediate alerting.
[08:48] Claire: Any gotchas around KV cache invalidation across regions? We use prefix caching in personalization.
[08:55] Jordan: Cross-region cache invalidation is tricky. We recommend region-local caches for hotpaths and fallback to recompute or serve stale for non-critical flows. We'll show cache topology options in the bench plan.
[09:08] Samir: If we need air-gapped on-prem in future, how much of Redwood runs on-prem vs control plane hosted?
[09:15] Jordan: We offer an on-prem package where inference nodes and a private control plane run in your network; telemetry and management can be optionally routed through our hosted control plane or self-hosted. We can discuss full air-gap options for regulated customers.
[09:28] Noah: Ok. About the audit trail again — we need retention windows and export formats for logs and traces.
[09:34] Jordan: Audit logs can be pushed to S3 or your SIEM, retention policy configurable. We'll include default retention and export format in the security pack.
[09:42] Maya: Quick recap — Tidal wants a pilot that: 1) validates hotpath failover for checkout and fraud pipelines, 2) measures failover time and correctness, 3) evaluates Dedicated vs Hosted latency/cost tradeoffs, 4) verifies security controls (KMS, SAML, logs).
[09:59] Samir: Correct. And we want a clear SLO mapping per route, plus runbook examples for common incidents.
[10:06] Jordan: We'll include runbook templates (region fail, node leak, model regression) in the bench deliverable.
[10:12] Claire: On timing — can we target the bench and initial results before our Q1 roadmap freeze? So before 2027-01-15?
[10:20] Maya: Tight but doable if we start bench next week. Jordan will draft the plan and Maya will follow up with pricing and security docs this week.
[10:28] Noah: Minor nit — can we get an example of a routing decision event payload so our SIEM can parse it?
[10:34] Jordan: Sure, we'll send a sample webhook JSON and a mapping doc.
[10:38] Samir: Anything else from Redwood?
[10:40] Maya: Not from me. Thanks everyone, we'll circulate action items and book the technical deep dive for late next week.
[10:47] Elena: Thanks.
[10:48] Noah: Thanks all.

End transcript.

References mentioned: Redwood security pack link (sent after call), bench plan template, runbook templates, sample webhook payload (will be attached).
